Chapter 3. Surviving the Famine: Scarcity, Loss, and Adaptation
Imagine the world you know suddenly turning upside down. That’s what happened in the 1990s, when a crisis swept across the country, changing millions of lives almost overnight.
The economy stumbled and, just like that, food started disappearing. The state, once so proud of providing for everyone, just couldn’t keep up its promises anymore. Rations grew smaller, then vanished altogether. Factories shut their doors, and the once-busy streets fell eerily silent. For so many people, just making it through the day became their whole world.
Picture a young boy—he used to run and play, but now he’s thin, quiet, always tired. His mom, who works in a factory, spends her days searching for anything edible. She stands in endless lines, trades with neighbors, even hunts for wild plants. Dinner shrinks to a little cornmeal or a watery soup. At night, that ache of hunger keeps them awake. The boy’s father, who once took pride in his role as a party member, feels completely powerless watching his family suffer.
Out in the countryside, things are even more grim. A farmer, no stranger to tough times, looks over his empty fields and waits for help that never comes. He watches as neighbors get sick, their bodies worn down from months of hunger. Some families have to make heartbreaking choices—selling their last possessions, sending their kids to beg, or leaving everything behind to search for food.
Hospitals, once a symbol of hope, become places people dread. Nurses do their best with almost nothing. They see patients arrive so weak they can barely stand, their bodies wasting away from starvation. With no medicine, barely any food, and not enough blankets to go around, all they can offer is kindness. The nurse learns to hide her sadness, focusing on small comforts.
The government responds with slogans and promises, but those words don’t fill empty stomachs. Publicly, they blame disasters and enemies abroad, but deep down, everyone knows the real story—years of poor decisions, isolation, and strict control have left the country unable to handle such a disaster. Those old certainties disappear, replaced by a day-to-day fight to survive.
But when support from above fades away, people start to adapt in unexpected ways. Take a woman who always followed the rules. Suddenly, she finds herself trading on the black market, bartering clothes for food, selling homemade things, learning to take risks she never imagined. She starts to see the limits of the system—and the power of her own choices.
Kids adapt, too. Some leave school to help their families—scavenging, working odd jobs, doing whatever they can. Others band together, roaming the streets in groups, searching for scraps to survive. Family bonds and community ties are tested like never before. Some people turn inward, just trying to get by. Others reach out, sharing what little they have with those even worse off.
These years leave deep wounds. So many lose loved ones—parents, children, friends. The sense of security from the state? It’s gone. Still, even in the hardest moments, there are flashes of resilience. A grandmother shares her last handful of rice with a hungry neighbor. A teacher keeps holding lessons, even when her students can barely sit upright. Through these small acts, the human spirit carries on.
As the crisis drags on, people start to question things they once took for granted. Those who always trusted the system begin to spot its cracks. The experience of hunger and loss plants something new—doubt, yes, but also a willingness to adapt and maybe, just maybe, hope for something better. In those quiet, everyday moments, the seeds of change start to grow.
